hints: Look carefully at the trace: when does the stem get thinner and when does it get fatter, daytime (12 00) or night-time (24 00)?
Think about what happens to water loss and pulling force in the xylem on a warm bright day, and how losing water from stem tissues would change diameter.
walkthrough:
**Read the pattern from the graph**

Look at the time axis first. The circumference falls during each daylight period and rises again during each night period. So the stem shrinks in the day and swells at night. This is a daily, reversible cycle.

**Link daytime to transpiration pull**

In the day, light and warmth open stomata and increase transpiration. Rapid evaporation from leaves pulls a fast transpiration stream up the xylem. This creates high tension (pulling force) in the water column due to cohesion between water molecules.

**Explain shrinking and swelling**

That strong daytime tension pulls water out of the surrounding living stem cells and elastic xylem vessels, so the whole stem contracts slightly. At night, transpiration almost stops, tension falls, cells re-fill with water and the circumference increases again. That matches option B exactly.

options.A: Adhesion of water to xylem walls does not switch off at night, and the stem actually swells at night, not shrinks.
options.B: High daytime transpiration increases cohesive tension in the xylem, withdrawing water from stem tissues so circumference falls, then recovery occurs at night.
options.C: Phloem mass flow does not cause this large daily shrink-swell cycle, and increased flow at night would not explain daytime shrinking.
options.D: Root pressure is mainly a night-time force when transpiration is low, and a fall in the day cannot explain the strong daytime tension and shrinkage.
